title: UK's Oldest Indian Restaurant Accuses Crown Estate of Cultural Ignorance in Eviction Row
excerpt: Veeraswamy, serving diners on London's Regent Street since 1926, is fighting the Crown Estate's refusal to renew its lease — a dispute whose court hearing has now been delayed until at least late autumn.
body:
• Veeraswamy, the UK's oldest Indian restaurant, has accused the Crown Estate of "cultural ignorance" as its eviction battle intensifies, The Telegraph reported.
  • The Michelin-starred restaurant has served diners on London's Regent Street since 1926 and is fighting the estate's refusal to renew its £205,000-a-year lease.
  • The five-day court hearing scheduled for June 29 was delayed for administrative reasons and is now unlikely to take place before late autumn 2026.
  • No closure yet: the pending legal case means Veeraswamy is still open at Victory House, 99 Regent Street — diners can still book a table while the fight continues.

Veeraswamy, the United Kingdom's oldest Indian restaurant, has accused the Crown Estate of "cultural ignorance" as its battle against eviction intensifies, The Telegraph reported. The Michelin-starred restaurant, which has served diners on London's Regent Street since 1926, is fighting the estate's refusal to renew its lease — a dispute that has now dragged on for more than a year.

MW Eat wants the court to let the restaurant stay in Victory House near Piccadilly Circus. The Crown Estate, which manages the monarch's portfolio and returns its profits to the Treasury, says it must reclaim the building for a comprehensive refurbishment of the upper-floor offices.

"I think it's an outrage. This is cultural philistinism."

— Ranjit Mathrani, chairman of MW Eat, to The Independent

Context & Background

Veeraswamy opened in April 1926 and is widely regarded as Britain's oldest surviving Indian restaurant. It was founded by the Indian-born Edward Palmer, the great-grandson of General William Palmer, military and private secretary to Warren Hastings, and the Mughal princess Faisan Nissa Begum. Palmer drew on recipes from Hyderabad's royal kitchens, learned from his great-grandmother.

When it opened, Indian restaurants were rare in Britain. Early customers included Anglo-Indians, civil servants and military figures with links to India, as well as Mahatma Gandhi and Jawaharlal Nehru. It later became a West End hotspot for royalty and stars from Charlie Chaplin to Queen Elizabeth II, and stayed open through the wartime Blitz. The owners claim the English habit of having a pint with a curry began at Veeraswamy, where the King of Denmark once had a cask of Carlsberg stored for his visits. The restaurant earned a Michelin star in 2016.

MW Eat, run by Mathrani with his sisters Namita and Camellia Panjabi, also operates the popular London Indian restaurants Chutney Mary and Amaya.

Impact & Analysis

The £205,000-a-year lease expired last summer after the Crown Estate decided against renewal, though the pending legal action has kept the restaurant open. The estate wants to knock down the wall separating the entrance to Veeraswamy from the entrance to the offices to create a larger reception for office tenants — a change it says would let it "materially increase" the rents it can charge. Without its own access, there is no restaurant.

Mathrani says refurbishment could be done with the restaurant in place — "a standard part of many similar refurbishments in London" — and that Veeraswamy proposed sharing the larger entrance and matching whatever rents the estate believes it could charge new tenants. The estate declined. MW Eat estimates relocating, fitting out a new site and closing during the move would cost around £5 million, and says the Crown Estate's offer of compensation would cover only a fraction.

"This is not a decision we've taken lightly," a Crown Estate spokesman has said, adding that the estate offered help finding new premises in its portfolio plus financial compensation. Mathrani, 83, called those claims "disingenuous" in a witness statement, saying nothing suitable had been offered and that the estate had "never been receptive to the notion of our restaurant staying in this building in any state."

Chefs including Raymond Blanc, Michel Roux, Richard Corrigan and Cyrus Todiwala signed an open letter in The Times calling the closure a cultural loss, and more than 20,000 signatures were delivered to Buckingham Palace urging King Charles to intervene.

Diaspora Angle

Few institutions embody a century of Indo-British cultural connection the way Veeraswamy does. It broke the ice for Indian dining in Britain when curry houses barely existed, fed generations of British Indian families, and turned the recipes of Hyderabad's royal kitchens into a fixture of London's West End. For the diaspora, the fight is about more than a lease: it is about whether a century-old Indian institution counts as heritage worth protecting when a commercial landlord wants the space back.

What's Next

The five-day hearing due to begin on June 29 at the Central London county court was delayed for "administrative reasons," The Times reported. Mathrani said new dates would follow but the hearing is unlikely before late autumn 2026, and that Veeraswamy "will make every effort to see if the dispute can be settled before" it. Until then, the restaurant keeps serving.
image_caption: A doorman in Veeraswamy uniform stands outside the restaurant’s facade at Victory House on Regent Street. The century-old restaurant is fighting the Crown Estate’s refusal to renew its lease, a dispute whose court hearing has been delayed until at least late autumn 2026.
nri_angle: A century-old Indian institution on London's Regent Street is fighting to survive against its royal landlord, making the case that Indian heritage in Britain deserves protection from commercial redevelopment.
